# The Desktop: Keeping Secrets Out of the Browser

Desktop applications built on web technology run a browser engine inside a
native window. That gives them a rendering stack, a layout engine, and a
large ecosystem, and it also gives them a browser engine's attack surface:
cross-site scripting, supply-chain compromise of a JavaScript dependency,
and a memory model in which a string, once created, may be copied by the
garbage collector and linger long after it is "deleted." For a program whose
purpose is to show people their passwords, that is the wrong place to keep
anything.

The FOKS desktop is built with Tauri, a framework that pairs a system
WebKit or WebView2 renderer with a Rust host process. This chapter is about
the arrangement that keeps key material and file contents out of the
renderer, and about a handful of engineering ideas that recur throughout the
host: generation counters, time-of-check-to-time-of-use races, digest-only
tracking, and bounded background work.

## Three tiers

```
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
|  WebKit renderer (React, TypeScript)              UNTRUSTED     |
|  - sees one revealed value at a time, on request               |
|  - never sees file bytes, vault keys, or signing keys          |
|  - can call: three Tauri core commands + app commands          |
+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
                               | Tauri IPC (JSON)
+------------------------------v--------------------------------+
|  Rust host (foks-desktop, Tauri)                  PRIVILEGED    |
|  - owns the window, dialogs, clipboard, drag-and-drop          |
|  - enforces the app lock on every value-bearing command        |
|  - streams file bytes between disk and the agent               |
+------------------------------+--------------------------------+
                               | Unix domain socket (foks-rs.sock)
+------------------------------v--------------------------------+
|  foks-agent (separate process)                    HOLDS KEYS    |
|  - all cryptography, all network sessions, all databases       |
|  - also serves the CLI and the MCP server                      |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
```

The renderer is treated as untrusted. It renders a catalog of names,
types, and sizes; it asks for one value at a time; and it receives that
value only through the single content-returning command. The host is
privileged but holds no long-lived secrets: it forwards requests to the
agent and moves bytes between the agent and the disk or clipboard. The
agent, described in [Chapter 19](19-agent.qmd), is a separate process that
outlives the window and that the command-line tool and the MCP server
([Chapter 21](21-mcp.qmd)) connect to as well.

## Exactly three core permissions

Tauri's capability model is an allowlist: a JSON file names which of the
framework's built-in commands a window's scripts may invoke. The default
set, `core:default`, expands to 92 commands, including
`core:image|from_path` (read any file the renderer names) and
`internal_toggle_devtools`. The FOKS capability file grants three:

| Permission | What it allows |
|---|---|
| `core:event:allow-listen` | subscribe to events the host emits |
| `core:event:allow-unlisten` | unsubscribe |
| `core:window:allow-start-dragging` | drag the window by its custom title bar |

Notably absent are `emit` and `emit_to`: the renderer cannot synthesize
events, so it cannot fake a file drop. The bundled dialog and clipboard
plugins are linked but granted no renderer permissions; only Rust drives
them.

A permission file is easy to get subtly wrong, so the project checks it by
test rather than by inspection. At build time Tauri generates an ACL
manifest describing every permission set and the commands each resolves to.
A unit test parses that generated manifest and the generated capability,
resolves each granted permission recursively to concrete
`manifest|command` pairs, and asserts the resulting set equals exactly the
three listed above. It then asserts a list of forbidden commands
(`core:image|from_path`, `core:path|resolve`,
`core:webview|internal_toggle_devtools`, `core:event|emit`, and others) is
unreachable. The project's permission notes give the reason this matters:
whether a command is *compiled in* is not the security boundary, because
Cargo feature unification across a workspace can pull in features a
sibling build enabled; only the capability file is a control, and only a
test that resolves it proves what it grants.

Application-defined commands are not covered by the capability file, so
every command that can return a value begins with two checks: that the
call came from the main window, and that the app is unlocked.

## The app lock: a generation counter

An *app lock* hides everything after a period of inactivity or on request,
and requires the person to authenticate before anything is shown again. The
subtle requirement is not the locking but what happens to work that was
already in flight. Suppose a multi-chunk download started, the app locked,
the person unlocked it, and the download's next chunk arrived. Is the app
unlocked? Yes. Should the download continue? No: the lock was meant to end
the session in which it was authorized.

A *generation counter* solves this. A monotonically increasing integer is
incremented on every lock; an operation records the generation when it
starts and, before doing anything sensitive, checks that the app is
unlocked *and* the generation is unchanged. A lock followed by an unlock
leaves the app unlocked but advances the generation, so the check fails.
The general pattern appears wherever "the same state" is not the same as
"a state that looks identical": caches invalidated by a version number,
optimistic concurrency by a version column, and so on.

In the host, `AppLock` holds a `locked` flag, a `generation` counter, and
an `authenticating` flag, all atomics. `lock()` sets the flag and
increments the generation. Long operations bracket themselves with two
calls:

```
g = unlocked_generation()          // read generation, require unlocked
... do work, possibly across many IPC round trips ...
require_unlocked_generation(g)     // require unlocked AND generation == g
```

A unit test named for the property, that locking invalidates work even
after unlock, pins it. The lock starts *engaged* on a platform that can
authenticate and *disengaged* on one that cannot, so the interface can
never become permanently inaccessible. Locking also scrubs: it invalidates
the cached catalog, closes any hosted-administration windows, and clears
delivered chat notifications. Unlocking uses `authenticating.swap(true)` so
a second prompt cannot open while one is pending.

### Delegating authentication to the operating system

FOKS has no master password. Authentication is delegated entirely to the
operating system, so the application never stores or compares a secret of
its own.

On macOS, the host asks `LAContext` whether biometric policy is available
(to label the mechanism "biometry" or "password") and then evaluates the
`DeviceOwnerAuthentication` policy, which accepts Touch ID, an Apple Watch,
or the account password. A 60-second timeout bounds the prompt, and the
three cancellation error codes (-2, -4, -9: user, system, and application
cancel) are reported as "not authenticated" rather than as failures.

On Linux, the host calls polkit over the system D-Bus. It first checks
that the action `com.aka.foks.desktop.unlock` is registered (the policy
file is installed by the package; if it is missing, the lock reports itself
unavailable rather than silently allowing). It then calls
`CheckAuthorization` with a *subject* of kind `unix-process` identified by
the host's PID and its **start time**, read as the 22nd field of
`/proc/<pid>/stat`. Including the start time matters because PIDs are
reused: a subject identified by PID alone could, after the original
process exits, name an unrelated process. The policy file sets
`allow_active=auth_self` and denies inactive and remote sessions, so only
the user at the active console can authenticate, and no administrator
privilege is involved.

## Time-of-check to time-of-use

A *TOCTOU* race is a bug in which a program checks a property of something
(a file, a process, a socket) and then acts on it, but the thing changes in
between. The check was correct when made and wrong when relied upon. The
defense is to make the check and the use atomic, or, when that is
impossible, to identify the thing by an unforgeable handle (an inode, a
process start time) and re-check that handle immediately before acting.

The host does this in several places. Before it launches the packaged
agent, it verifies the binary is a regular file (not a symlink), owned by
the same user as the desktop, not writable by group or world, and
executable. When it finds an incompatible agent already bound to the
socket, it reads the peer's PID from the socket (`LOCAL_PEERPID` on macOS,
`SO_PEERCRED` on Linux), shows the person a confirmation dialog naming
that process, and then **re-inspects the socket after the dialog closes**.
If the endpoint no longer matches what was shown, no signal is sent, since
approval applied only to the endpoint originally displayed. The polkit
start-time subject above is the same idea applied to processes.

## Clipboard hygiene

Copying a password to the clipboard hands it to every clipboard-history
tool on the machine. The host's `copy_with_hygiene` does three things:

1. It computes `SHA-256(value)` and a generation number, writes the value
   to the pasteboard, and then drops the zeroizing string. Only the 32-byte
   digest and the generation are kept in memory.
2. A thread sleeps for the auto-clear interval and then calls
   `clear_if_unchanged`: it reads the current clipboard text, hashes it,
   and clears the clipboard **only if the digest still matches**. A value
   the person copied in the meantime is never destroyed. The generation
   ensures a repeated copy of the same value gets its own timer.
3. On macOS it also sets the `org.nspasteboard.ConcealedType` pasteboard
   type, a convention that asks clipboard managers not to record the item.
   Linux has no equivalent, which is why its timer is shorter.

| Platform | Auto-clear |
|---|---|
| Linux | 15 s |
| macOS and others | 30 s |

The exit handler performs one best-effort clear before the process ends.

## Files: drag-and-drop, upload, and download

A web `<input type="file">` reads bytes into a JavaScript buffer. FOKS
wants uploads without bytes in the renderer, but it also must not turn a
"path-taking" command into a general file reader that the renderer could
point at any file on disk.

The drop event lands in Rust, because Tauri's `dragDropEnabled` routes it
to the host. `record_drop_paths` accepts **exactly one** UTF-8 path as
authorized; a multi-file drop is reported for display but authorizes
nothing. The renderer then calls `upload_path` with the path string it was
shown, and the host looks it up in the pending set: a path that was not
dropped, or was already consumed, yields `drop-not-authorized`. Paths
chosen through the native picker never cross the IPC boundary at all. The
host rejects symlinks and non-regular files, then streams the file to the
agent in frames of at most 700 KiB, the agent protocol's payload bound
from [Chapter 17](17-wire.qmd), each held in a zeroizing buffer. A transcript
test carries an 84 MiB sparse file through the backend and confirms it
travels only as bounded frames.

Download reverses the path with three properties: atomicity, integrity,
and no plaintext left behind on failure. The host opens the native save
dialog itself, creates a temporary file **in the destination's directory**
(so the final rename is on one filesystem), and streams chunks from the
agent, validating that each chunk's store, path, version, and offset match
the request and that the running total stays under the limit. Each chunk
buffer is zeroized after it is written. When the agent signals end of
file, the total length is compared to the item's authenticated size; a
mismatch is a `response-binding` error. Then `sync_all` flushes the file
and `persist` renames it into place, which POSIX guarantees is atomic. A
crash at any earlier point leaves a temporary file, never a partial file
under the chosen name.

| Bound | Value |
|---|---|
| Inline KV write threshold (above this, stream) | 128 KiB |
| Stream frame | 700 KiB |
| In-memory reveal | 16 MiB |
| Download | 1 GiB |

The repository's HTML guide states the download limit as 512 MB; the code
defines 1 GiB, and the code is authoritative.

## The agent's lifecycle

The host launches the packaged agent with `--request-timeout-seconds 60`
(the agent's default of 15 s is too short for a path that may raise a
blocking macOS Keychain prompt), with standard input closed and standard
output and error redirected to a 0600 log file. A reaper thread waits on
the child so its exit status is observed. Exit is a one-way state machine
in the close guard, `Idle → Decision → Stopping → Finalizing`, with `Failed`
and `ForceConfirmation` branches, and the desktop process ends only after
the agent's termination has been verified; the state cannot move backward
from `Finalizing`.

## The notification consumer

The chat view must discover new messages across every channel of every
team without flooding the agent, while the conversation the person is
looking at must never feel stale. The consumer that does this is a small
exercise in bounded background work.

**Round-robin from a persisted cursor.** Each pass walks the inbox snapshot
in two segments starting at `cursor % size`, so the walk resumes where the
last one stopped rather than restarting at channel zero and starving the
channels at the end. The walk allocates no channel array.

**Bounds and budgets.**

| Bound | Value |
|---|---|
| Queued jobs | 64 |
| Progress records (baselines) | 4,096 |
| Rows per pass | 400 |
| Bytes per pass | 4 MiB |
| Rows per channel read | 100 |
| Bytes per channel read | 1 MiB |
| Evictions per 5 s window | 64 |

When the progress table is full, the consumer evicts an idle record before
admitting a new channel, but caps evictions per 5-second window so that
rotation "must not become an endless baseline RPC loop." Before starting a
job it reserves a whole channel read against the pass budget; a budget
miss re-arms after a short yield.

**Geometric backoff, with one exception.** A channel whose pass found
nothing new doubles its interval from 5 s toward a ceiling of 60 s; a
pass that observed a newer sequence resets it to 5 s. The module
documentation is explicit about what this trades: on a degraded host, a
message in a quiet, unopened channel may be noticed up to 60 s after it
arrives rather than up to 5 s. No message is skipped; the backoff decides
when the read happens, not whether. **The channel whose thread is open
never backs off**: the due-time computation uses the base interval whenever
the channel is the presented one, whatever interval is stored. Opening a
channel that had backed off therefore makes it due at the base interval
immediately.

Timers are armed for the earliest computed deadline, or not at all if
nothing is due; other wake-ups come from inbox publications or admission
releases. Baselines are seeded from the inbox projection's own head when it
is not degraded, costing no request.

## History paging

Chat history is paged with an opaque `before` cursor: a history reply
carries `messages`, `before` (the cursor for older rows, or null), and the
integrity fields `missing_predecessors` and `gap` described in
[Chapter 16](16-chat.qmd). An incremental refresh asks for rows `after`
the newest sequence held; if the reply reports a gap, the view falls back
to a full first page and replaces what it held.

A *published-head gate* avoids a class of wasted requests. The inbox
snapshot carries a `head` sequence per channel, and the decoder enforces
that `cursor <= head` and that `degraded` is true exactly when they
differ. When a revision arrives for a reason other than a new message,
the tail read is skipped if the published head is not beyond the newest
held sequence, because the server would only confirm that nothing newer
exists.

The history cache is a least-recently-used map keyed by a binding of
store, channel, scope, generation, and authority, bounded at 16 channels,
1,000 rows, and 8 MiB. Reading an entry re-inserts it to refresh recency.
A binding whose authority or generation has changed is simply not
current, so a page fetched under an old role cannot be shown after the
role changes. The row and byte limits come from the shared
`chat-limits.json` of [Chapter 24](24-performance.qmd).

## Vault edits

Items and folders offer Rename or move within their current vault. The target
is an exact absolute path under an existing folder, and a live destination
is never overwritten. The selected source version remains fixed across retries.

Delete folder is available for real nonroot folders and is empty-only. It
requires the server's atomic empty-directory extension, whose transaction
checks concurrent children before removing the source. Unsupported servers
are refused before a removal is prepared. The desktop exposes no recursive
folder deletion.

The card grid windows whole rows at the current viewport width through
`files-grid.ts`, so it can scroll through the full loaded catalog without
mounting every card. It no longer imposes the former 200-card cap.
